newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-APEC seen needing $1.6 trillion energy funds.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-APEC seen needing $1.6 trillion energy funds.

text.p: About US$1.6 trillion in investment capital is needed to meet the energy growth demand of the Asia-Pacific region over the next 10 years, Australian Resources and Energy Minister Warwick Parer said on Tuesday.
In remarks to reporters after addressing Asia-Pacific energy ministers in Sydney, Parer said the funding required was too much for governments to bear on their own.
"It's a figure that no governments can handle on their own," Parer said. "It will need private sector investment."
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Ltd earlier on Tuesday identified to the ministers several obstacles blocking construction of new power generating plants in Asia and Oceania.
If these obstacles can be overcome, Mitsubishi sees over half the new capacity for generating power worldwide being built in Asia and Oceania.

Power generated in Asia under the Independent Power Scheme (IPP) electric utility privatisation effort would represent 65 percent of capacity among new plants slated to be built over the next three years in 10 countries, Yasuo Nakagami, the company's managing director, said in a paper delivered to the ministers.
Moreover, most of the new coal-fired projects planned would be built in the two regions, Nakagami said.
"There are, however, several 'impedimental issues' that need to be resolved before the projects can be built," he said.
Laws and regulations are not well established for accommodating the power scheme and a framework for equity and loans does not exist, Nakagami said.
"It actually takes a long time to close the finance of IPP projects due to those reasons," Nakagami said.
While IPP projects are gaining in popularity because they allow for effective use of foreign capital, laws and regulations in host countries are not well established, he said.
Nakagami called on all parties to share in the risks of the projects in an "equitable and reasonable manner."
Parer said Australia stood to benefit from higher private investment in the Asian energy sector due to its role as a net exporter of energy sources such as uranium, gas and coal.
Parer also said he hoped Australia could play a greater role as a supplier of uranium to South Korea as that country builds more nuclear power plants.
A South Korean official said earlier this week that the country plans to build 19 nuclear plants.

The minister said that while China was a much larger producer of coal than Australia, most Chinese coal was consumed domestically, while Australia exports between 80 percent and 90 percent of its output.
The 18 countries in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation zone consume about half the world's energy, Parer said.
A 14-point plan to be reviewed by APEC energy ministers later this week, would if approved make investment regimes for energy more attractive, he said.
